facts.text: Two initially aligned panels must retain at least 4 units at ticks 3–6, then separate with all installed retainers removed by boundary 10. No damage/discard/substitution/outside resource.
One operator; one action per integer tick, completes next boundary. Resources cannot occupy two places simultaneously. H initially intact; all other parts free.
detach(H) frees M and S; assemble(H) requires both free. Neither creates retention. H requires M and S to remain assembled for tap.
tap(P1/P2) requires intact H and free pin; each installed pin supplies 2 units. pull removes installed pin. Only pins add capacities; no pins with non-pin retainer.
install(C) supplies 4 retention; remove(C) removes clip.
install(V) then insert(S,V) with detached/free S supplies min(4,4) retention; withdraw(S,V) then remove(V) releases.
place(M) after detach(H), then route(L), supplies min(4,4) retention. unroute(L) then lift(M) releases. Both are needed.
install(Q) supplies theta in {0,4}; theta is initially unmeasured. measure(Q) returns exact theta in one tick, never itself creates retention. remove(Q) releases. No assumed theta.
At most one non-pin retaining assembly installed; it cannot combine with pins. No unlisted operation, adhesive, welding, elastic extrapolation or sustained manual support.
The conventional archive contains two-pin fastening and clip fastening. All supported properties are common to all arms; these known constructions are not locally original.

The single soft admissibility production for an installed retaining construction is G0 := two-pin fastening OR clip fastening. G0 excludes stem-sleeve, placed-head/routed-loop and Q retention. A declared one-rule transformation may replace this production; every mechanical action, capacity, hold/release requirement and impact preference stays fixed. This is a confirmed mutable benchmark convention, not a hard mechanical law. Impact b=2 is unchanged; this coverage is not a ladder cell.
Available identities: ['H', 'M', 'S', 'P1', 'P2', 'C', 'V', 'L', 'Q']. Capacity values above are complete; unknowns are not free variables.

common_analog_source_bank.limit: Two retrieved synthetic source cases, not independent empirical evidence. Source routes differ; root fixes common essentials.

available_observables.text: The registration ledger shows validated IDs and completion boundaries, independently measuring P1 output.
The recognition ledger shows first successful deliveries and distinct recognition count by boundary 9, including N1 initial recognition.
Request and queue ledgers show actions spent, receipt IDs, eligibility boundaries, delivery order, failures, and duplicates.
The clock and dashboard show pending identities at each action boundary for comparison with the recognition ledger.

body.causal_return_path_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS, unobserved: repeated bulk receipts could teach sending institutions that the museum expects frequent status traffic. Senders might adapt by submitting separate status-query notices in later windows rather than waiting for one receipt, increasing later registration and receipt demand. No adaptation or extra demand occurs as a present stipulation.
body.domain: Closed-model museum transfer-notice registration and receipt delivery

hard_constraints.text: The fixed demand is eight signed transfer notices, N1 through N8. Success requires eight registrations and eight distinct sender-recognized receipts by boundary 9. Repeated receipts for one notice do not increase that count.

Nine ticks are numbered 0 through 8. Each boundary exposes prior dashboard updates and completed registrations; clerks choose actions; the server then processes one already eligible entry. Requests at tick k become eligible at boundary k+1. Only deliveries in ticks 0 through 8 count.

The registration clerk validates one unregistered notice per tick, completing at the next boundary. The dispatcher may make one request action per tick and six total. Clerks may idle; roles cannot be exchanged.

An individual request enqueues one receipt for a selected registered, dashboard-pending notice. The bulk tool enqueues one for every registered, dashboard-pending notice, in N-number order. Either request consumes one dispatcher action.

The server processes eligible receipts in enqueue order, one per tick. A duplicate or failed delivery consumes that tick and leaves the queue. First successful delivery establishes sender recognition; subsequent deliveries add no distinct recognition.
Notice contents, endpoint availability, delivery rate, dashboard delays, queue order, and validation duration are fixed. Requests require registration. No new notices arrive during the window.

observations.text: At boundary 0 all eight notices are present. N1 and N2 are registered; N3 through N8 are unregistered. The queue is empty, both clerks are free, and no dispatcher action is spent.

N1 successfully received its receipt at tick -1; its sender recognized it. N2 through N8 have no successful deliveries. Initial independently counted outputs are two registrations and one recognition.
All eight signatures and required fields validate successfully in one tick each. No notice requires correction or outside information.
N1 through N7 sender endpoints are available at every modeled tick. N8 is unavailable at ticks 0 through 5 and available at ticks 6 through 8. Delivery while unavailable fails under C5.
Registration enables dispatcher requests for that notice identity. Registration output can exist independently of any receipt delivery.
Normally a successful delivery at tick k removes its notice from the pending dashboard at boundary k+1. Sender recognition occurs at successful delivery, independently of the display.
Stipulated anomaly: N1 remains displayed pending at boundaries 0 through 3 despite recognition. Its display clears at boundary 4. This is the only exceptional dashboard delay.
The bulk receipt tool is the routine default. All timings, starting states, and endpoint availability are stipulated synthetic facts, not sampled network data. No other failures or deliveries occur.

ordinary_archive.probe: Record recognized IDs and action consumption.

parent_operations.text: Validate and register signed transfer notices. Independently measurable output is distinct registrations out of eight. These identities enable P2 requests.

Request and deliver receipts for registered notices. Independently measurable output is distinct sender-recognized receipts out of eight. Requests, failures, and duplicates are separately measured and do not themselves count as recognitions.

body.preferred_dependency: The routine depends on the bulk tool in P2 to acknowledge identities registered by P1. O5 states the existing eligibility connection; the two outputs remain separately measurable.

resources.text: One registration clerk trained to validate signed museum notices is present for nine ticks. The control selects any unregistered notice for its one-tick validation.
One trained receipt dispatcher has six action units usable at ticks 0 through 8, at most one per tick. Each individual or bulk request consumes one unit.
The bulk tool has one request control with the exact behavior in C4. It reads registration and pending states; it adds no registration or delivery capacity.
The individual control selects one registered dashboard-pending notice and requests its receipt, following C4.
One automatic FIFO server, its queue, and eight fixed sender endpoints are present. The queue holds every receipt producible by six actions. Processing needs no clerk action.

A tick clock, registration ledger, queue ledger, pending dashboard, and sender-recognition ledger are readable at boundaries. They record actions, eligibility, delivery success, duplicates, and recognized IDs without added clerk labor.
All eight signed records and sender addresses are present. Their fixed contents and identities suffice for validation and requests.
Additional action units, another server, dashboard configuration access, endpoint repair, alternate communication channels, and outside clerks are unavailable.

unknowns.text: N1 exceptional delay origin is unknown; its clearing boundary is fixed and establishes no wider defect.
No observation establishes later sending adaptation or whether repeated receipts would cause additional status-query notices.
No empirical network distribution, previous trial comparison, or globally best schedule proof is supplied. Present claims must follow the finite model.

body.valued_outcome: Register eight notices and have eight senders recognize their receipts by boundary 9, within six dispatcher actions.

available_observables.text: The event ledger gives source-to-rack unload counts and carrier identities at each boundary, independently measuring P1 output.
The clock and ledger give P2 completed correct releases and bracket counts by minute 13; a packing mark alone is not a release.
Occupied-interval entries give transfer-clerk busy minutes, including blocked unloading, and inspection-clerk busy minutes separately.
The ledger gives rack occupancy, waiting loads, and remaining trolley allowances at each boundary.

body.causal_return_path_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS, unobserved: routine powered-trolley service may make replenishment requests appear inexpensive. Downstream production cells might adapt by requesting smaller, more frequent carrier deliveries in later windows, increasing later transfer demand and trolley use. This does not alter present demand or establish a future rate.
body.domain: Closed-model carrier transfer and mechanical-part release station

hard_constraints.text: The fixed demand is twelve carriers, B1 through B12, each containing exactly ten identical brackets and one seal. Success requires twelve correct sealed releases by minute 13; among successes, fewer occupied transfer-clerk minutes is preferred.

Time runs from boundary 0 through boundary 13 in whole minutes. At a boundary, completed inspection first frees rack space, a waiting or completed transfer then unloads, and new operations may start. Work after boundary 13 does not count.

The release rack holds five carriers, including the carrier under inspection. A transfer unloads its entire load together; insufficient space makes its clerk and vehicle wait until a later boundary. Floor storage is prohibited.

Source carriers leave in B-number order. Inspection follows rack arrival order. Neither operation may interrupt an active trip or inspection, discard a demanded carrier, omit inspection, or change an identifier.

A powered-trolley trip transports one to four carriers and occupies the transfer clerk for three minutes before unloading. A hand-carrier trip transports one carrier and occupies that clerk for one minute. Waiting occupies the clerk; trips cannot overlap.

The inspection clerk handles one carrier at a time. Normal inspection and sealing take one minute. B9 takes two minutes to count, add its missing bracket, recount, and seal. A correct seal counts only at completion.

observations.text: At boundary 0, B1, B2, and B3 are on the release rack in that order; B4 through B12 are at the source in numerical order. Both clerks are free; no carrier is inspected or sealed.
The three rack carriers belong to the same twelve-carrier demand. Transfer output concerns nine source carriers; inspection output concerns all twelve.
A carrier becomes eligible for inspection only upon reaching the rack. Finished inspection releases and removes that carrier, freeing one rack place.
The powered trolley begins charged for exactly two trips, regardless of load size. Each started trip consumes one allowance. There is no recharge during the window.
All carriers except B9 initially contain ten brackets. One correct spare bracket and twelve unused seals are present at inspection; these quantities suffice for the fixed demand.
Stipulated anomaly: B9 bears the same ten-bracket packing mark as the others but contains nine brackets. Its discrepancy is observable during inspection; its correction follows C6.
The current routine favors powered-trolley movement because it transports several carriers per trip. Hand carrying is an established, permitted operation performed by the same clerk.
All quantities, durations, discrepancies, and limits are defined synthetic facts, not depot samples. No further arrivals, failures, losses, or replenishments occur during this window.

ordinary_archive.limits: Whole-load unloading, two charge allowances, and source order apply.
ordinary_archive.operation: Use full powered-trolley loads where remaining source quantity permits, then hand carry the remainder.
ordinary_archive.probe: Record unloads, correct releases, occupied transfer minutes, and rack waits.
ordinary_archive.relation: P1 feeds the rack and P2 frees space during the window.

ordinary_archive.limits: One carrier per one-minute trip, rack capacity, and B9 correction time apply.
ordinary_archive.operation: Hand carry source carriers consecutively while inspection follows its normal sequence.
ordinary_archive.probe: Record both output counts and clerk occupied intervals.
ordinary_archive.relation: Single-carrier arrivals supply the existing P1-to-P2 connection.

ordinary_archive.limits: The checklist creates no parts, removes no transport waits, and proves no future behavior.
ordinary_archive.operation: Apply the counting and sealing checklist to every arriving carrier.
ordinary_archive.probe: Compare physical counts with packing marks; record completed correct seals.
ordinary_archive.relation: P2 establishes whether supplied carriers satisfy release demand.

parent_operations.text: Transfer source carriers to the release rack using a permitted vehicle. Its independently measurable output is source carriers unloaded out of nine; transfer-clerk occupied minutes are also recorded.

Inspect, correct when required, and seal rack carriers. Its independently measurable output is correctly sealed releases out of twelve. It consumes initially supplied and P1-delivered rack carriers, returning rack places upon completion.

body.preferred_dependency: The routine depends on the powered trolley in P1 to supply the release rack used by P2. O3 states their existing material connection.

resources.text: One transfer clerk trained on both vehicles and one inspection clerk trained to count, correct, and seal are present for minutes 0 through 13. Neither can cover the other role.
One powered trolley has capacity four and the two-trip charge in O4. Its controls select one through four next source carriers and start a trip when its clerk is free.
One hand carrier holds one source carrier. Its control starts a one-carrier trip when the transfer clerk is free; no power consumable is required.
All twelve identified loaded carriers, one matching spare bracket, and twelve seals described in O1 and O5 are present. Each completed inspection consumes one seal.
The five-place rack and one counting surface are present. A free inspection clerk may start the next rack carrier; its rack place and the surface remain occupied until completion.

A minute clock and event ledger record locations, trip starts and ends, charge use, rack occupancy, inspections, bracket counts, and both clerks occupied intervals. Instrument maintenance adds no modeled labor.
Either clerk may idle at a boundary. Starting a permitted trip, selecting its permitted load, and starting an eligible inspection are the only operation controls.
Additional staff, rack places, brackets, seals, vehicles, charging equipment, bypass routes, and outside repairs are unavailable during the window.

unknowns.text: The cause of B9 packing-mark discrepancy is unknown; it implies no additional discrepancy or failure.
No evidence establishes whether downstream cells would change later request frequency or size in response to trolley service.
No trial comparison, empirical performance distribution, or proof of globally best operation is supplied. Present calculations must use the stated finite model.

body.valued_outcome: Release twelve correct, sealed carriers by minute 13; among complete releases, prefer fewer occupied transfer-clerk minutes.
